newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says 250-300 buried in Andean mudslide.
newsitem.headline: Peru says 250-300 buried in Andean mudslide.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Wednesday a vast mudslide that swept off an Andean mountainside over two remote villages had buried between 250 and 300 people in its wake.

"This is a disaster with very serious consequences. It has literally buried two communities where there were approximately 100 families," Fujimori told local radio station Radioprogramas del Peru from the site of the disaster.
"We calculate that there are between 250 and 300 people buried under this immense amount of mud that we are seeing here," he said.
He added that 41 bodies had been recovered so far, although an official at the local headquarters of the rescue operation had earlier put the figure at 47.
Fujimori said there were "few survivors" from the tragedy and warned there was a "huge mass" of mud at the site that could slide if it rains again.
The mountainside in southeastern Peru collapsed before dawn on Tuesday, deluging the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra at its foot with a torrent of mud and rocks.
Inhabitants had been evacuated after weekend flooding, but their refuge in a fold of the mountain above the village put them in the path of the mudslide.
Fujimori said emergency aid was being brought to the "really few" survivors and a large number of soldiers were working with picks, spades and their bare hands to pull out bodies.
A Reuters correspondent at the village of Kerapata beside the mudslide said Fujimori looked grim-faced, brushed aside most reporters and hugged several weeping villagers.

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer, accompanying Fujimori, warned of epidemics among what he estimated as between 250 and 600 families left homeless by the mudslide, other flooding and smaller slides in the same vicinity.

As Fujimori visited the zone, Civil Defence chief Gen. Homero Nurena arrived in the nearby city of Cuzco to direct operations assisted by 300 soldiers, and to evacuate other villages threatened by heavy seasonal rains.
"We are going to be evacuating people from the area who are in danger," Nurena told Reuters.

Authorities in Abancay, capital of the stricken Apurimac department, said 33 deaths had been confirmed late on Tuesday by the time darkness, fog and further small landslides forced rescuers to call off the search for more bodies.
After a delay because of early morning fog on Wednesday, scores of firemen, soldiers, police and volunteers resumed the grim task of finding bodies before the mud dried.
Congressman Dennis Vargas Marin, who comes from the area and flew there to assess damage, said as many as 350 people had disappeared.

Rescue workers pulled dozens of bodies from the mud, many mutilated. "There were arms, heads, pieces of bodies sticking out of the mud," said one firefighter. "We have tried to dig up the bodies using picks and shovels, but it's been difficult."
Local leaders called on the government to declare a state of emergency for the devastated area.

"I was in the zone, and honestly everything was destroyed. There were people weeping and trying desperately to move the mud," Lt. Manuel Gonzales, of the region's military authority, said. "We are taking tents and food now for the more than 100 people who have nothing."
Civil Defence was sending 18 tons of supplies including food and blankets to the region as well as three dogs to help find bodies.

Flash floods, mudslides and landslides, known locally as "huaycos", are common in Peru's Andes during the January-March rainy season. But Congressman Jubert Chavez Serrano, who also flew to the scene, said: "It's the worst tragedy of this kind we have seen in many years. We had some big 'huaycos' 20 or 30 years ago, but never like this."
The tragedy capped five deaths from flooding in Tamburco this weekend and three in the jungle province of Rioja where at least 750 families' homes were swept away by floods.
In one of the worst disasters in Peru's history, an earthquake in 1970 set off land movements that buried 70,000 people in the Andean town of Yungay and its surrounding areas.
